title: The Six Cases
subtitle: Nominative subject; accusative object; genitive possession; dative indirect object; ablative everything else; vocative direct address.
objectives: Identify the function of each of the six cases.
Translate sentences using all six cases.
Recognize case by ending and function by context.
Understand the ablative as the catch-all case for means, manner, place, time, agent.

sections.heading: The six cases and their functions
sections.body:
Latin has six cases. Each signals a different function in the sentence.

1. Nominative: the subject. puella cantat. — The girl sings.
2. Genitive: possession, or 'of'. filia puellae. — The daughter of the girl.
3. Dative: indirect object, or 'to/for'. puellae rosam dō. — I give a rose to the girl.
4. Accusative: direct object. puellam videō. — I see the girl.
5. Ablative: means, manner, place, time, agent, accompaniment. cum puellā. — with the girl. ā puellā. — by the girl.
6. Vocative: direct address. puella, venī! — Girl, come!

The ablative is the most versatile. It does the work of several English prepositions: by, with, from, in, at, on.

sections.heading: Examples from Cicero and Caesar
sections.body:
Cicero writes: salūs populī suprēma lēx estō. — Let the safety of the people be the supreme law. 'populī' is genitive singular, modifying 'salūs'. 'lēx' is nominative singular, subject of 'estō'.

Caesar writes: cum legiōnibus in Galliam vēnit. — He came into Gaul with the legions. 'legiōnibus' is ablative plural, accompaniment. 'Galliam' is accusative singular, motion towards.

Cicero writes: ō tempora, ō mōrēs! — O the times, O the customs! 'tempora' and 'mōrēs' are vocative/accusative (the vocative is often identical to the nominative for plurals and neuters).
